When Phainon woke up, he screamed.

The pounding in his head was unbearable, and his skin burned as if it were cracking under invisible pressure—but that wasn’t what made him scream.

For one, his professor was terrifyingly close to his face, his expression twisted into a scowl so deep it could’ve been carved there. That alone was enough to make Phainon flinch.

For another, he had no clothes.

“Oh. He’s awake.”

Phainon scrambled to cover himself, though the thin blanket did little to hide anything. He glanced around in panic. Anaxa was standing now, exhaling a soft sigh that could easily have gone unnoticed. Beside him stood—

“Mydeimos, he should be cleared. Just let me know if the cracks get any worse.”

“So he’s just… fine?” Mydei had this incredulous look on his face, glancing between Phainon and Anaxa.

Phainon coughed, “Hey so what happened?? And where are my clothes—”

“Yes. Surprisingly enough, the process was easier than I anticipated. For some reason, his soul simply accepted the procedure. I expected resistance —or rejection.”

“…And yet you still did it? Without telling anyone? What would’ve happened if his soul rejected you? What then?”

“Guys, please—”

“I would have used my own soul. It isn’t unheard of within my capabilities. Did you think I’d simply stop if he resisted?”

“Not a chance. A scholar like you would never. You’d see it as a challenge —and for that, I’ve always respected you.” “My… my clothes…” Phainon sighed, lowering his gaze.

His body was still marked by those strange cracks—pale, jagged lines tracing across his arms and legs like fractured glass. They looked almost like scars, though far worse. The deep gash across his chest had sealed into an ugly golden mark that drew his attention immediately.

It burned, just as it always had since his cycles of memory began—but now, something felt different…alost wrong or like a piece of him was missing…?

The small blanket draped over his legs offered little comfort. Thankfully, it was only Mydei and Anaxa in the room—both too caught up in their own conversation to notice his discomfort. Talking. Or maybe arguing. No, judging by Anaxa’s calm expression, probably just talking.

And yet… a moment ago he could hear them clearly. Now their voices came through only in fragments—sharp bursts fading into silence if they spoke too softly.

…His hearing really was getting worse, wasn’t it?

“—And Hyacine. You owe her a lot.”

Anaxa’s face fell slightly; guilt flickered across his features. “In due time —”

“You mean now?”

“I will apologize. She didn’t deserve the kind of mental torment she endured.”

“Do any of us?”

“Are you speaking as an insult to me, or as a reflection on all of us?”

Mydei huffed. “Both.”

Anaxa’s gaze drifted toward Phainon again. For a moment, his expression softened, then hardened back into something more guarded—judgmental, almost. “I’ll leave you two alone. And, Crown Prince, be gentle with him.”

“Hey, what’s that supposed to—”

But Anaxa was already gone, coat sweeping dramatically behind him as he turned on his heel. “Phainon?”

The man’s eyes flicked toward Phainon—soft, worried. No… not worried. Relieved.

“How are you feeling?” His voice was low, quiet, and disgustingly gentle.

“Naked.”

“Other than that?”

“Exposed.”

“Hks—your clothes are right there.”

Phainon quickly grabbed them, tugging the fabric over his still-marked skin. When he looked up, Mydei’s gaze hadn’t moved. His eyes were still locked on him.

“And how are you feeling Mydeimos?”

“What…?”

“You asked me. Can I not ask the same?”

“I’m fine.”

Phainon doubted it. He knew Mydei better than he knew himself sometimes —he just knew.

“Mydeimos, do you take me for a fool—”

“You almost died.”

“…I did?”

“Yes. You— you almost died.” Mydei repeated it as though saying it twice might make it real. His voice wavered despite himself. “Professor Anaxagoras said that if you’d burned any further, your soul would have been damaged beyond repair. Not wounded. Not scarred. Gone.”

Phainon swallowed any argument he had.  “I… I’m sorry,” he said at last. “But if I had to choose between you all and myself, I would—”

“Choose us all,” Mydei snapped. “By Nikador, Deliverer, you piss me off.”

Phainon startled, then frowned. “That wasn’t—”

“No, don’t.” Mydei dragged a hand through his hair, pacing once before stopping again, fists clenched. “Do you have any idea what it’s like to stand there and be told you were seconds away from ceasing to exist? To hear that and realize I wouldn’t even have been able to stop you?”

Silence stretched between them.

“You don’t get to make that choice alone,” Mydei continued, quieter now but no less fierce. “You don’t get to decide that your life is worth less than ours just because you’re willing to suffer for it.”

Phainon looked at him then. Really looked. The anger. The fear underneath it.

“I wasn’t trying to be brave,”

Mydei exhaled sharply. “And that’s supposed to make it better?”

For a moment, Mydei said nothing. Then he stepped closer, close enough that Phainon could feel the residual heat of him.

“Next time,” Mydei said, voice low, controlled only by effort, “you choose to live. Even if it’s selfish. Even if it hurts. Even if you think we’d be better off without you.”

Phainon’s chest tightened.

“…Okay,” he said.

Mydei searched his face, clearly unconvinced, then scoffed under his breath. “You’re impossible.”

Phainon smiled faintly. “And yet.”

“And yet,” Mydei echoed, turning away again, “you’re still here.”

He let out a long sigh. Phainon took that as his cue to busy himself, smoothing down his sleeves and tugging his collar into place. It was something to do with his hands. Something to break the awkward weight that had settled between them.

Cyrene’s voice echoed faintly in his memory, sharp and far too observant.

“You two still a thing?”

Phainon wasn’t sure.

He’d spent so long just… recovering. Existing. Breathing from one moment to the next without thinking beyond it. He hadn’t expected to get this far at all. Hadn’t expected to be standing here, alive, with Mydei close enough to feel the heat from him.

He coughed softly, trying to clear his head. Strangely, it worked. Too well.

His thoughts felt clear. Unusually so. He blinked, a quiet unease settling in his chest. Something was off. It was as if his soul felt lighter, unburdened in a way that didn’t sit right. Not relief. Not peace. Just… less.

“Phainon.”

Mydei’s voice was closer now. When Phainon looked up, Mydei’s hand was resting over his wrist. Not gripping. Just there, warm and grounding.

“Are you done?”

“Y—yeah,” Phainon said, a little breathless.

Mydei huffed a word under his breath, something in Kremnoan that Phainon didn’t quite catch, then nodded once. “Then let’s go.”

“To where?” Phainon wondered distantly Mydei huffed again. “Food, I guess.”

Phainon visibly winced. The thought alone made his mouth ache, memory supplying phantom heat, the way even water had burned against his tongue earlier. He swallowed and nodded anyway.

They walked for a few steps before Mydei spoke again, slower this time, as if choosing his words carefully.

“You asked what happened,” he said. “I didn’t answer properly.”

Phainon glanced at him. “I didn’t ask.”

“You would have,” Mydei replied. “Eventually.”

He exhaled through his nose. “Anaxagoras was the first to notice something was wrong. Not just exhaustion. Not just overuse. He said you felt… hollow. Like it was eating inward.”

Phainon’s brow furrowed. “Hollow?”

“Burning,” Mydei corrected. “From the inside out.”

He stopped walking then, turning fully toward Phainon. His expression was tight, controlled only by effort.

“Anaxagoras said your body wasn’t failing. Your soul was.”

Phainon’s breath hitched before he could stop it.

“You’d burned through too much of it,” Mydei continued. “Used it as fuel when your reserves ran dry. Your body tried to keep up anyway. That’s when it started to decay. Not rot. Decay. Like something burning without flame.”

Phainon felt cold all at once.

“So Anaxa…” he started.

“Ripped his own soul out,” Mydei said flatly.

Phainon stopped short. “oh.”

“Not all of it,” Mydei said, sharp. “Enough. He tore off a fragment and bound it to yours to stabilize you. Anchored you long enough to stop the collapse.”

The words settled heavily between them.

“He said it should hold,” Mydei added. “For now. But he can’t monitor it closely. Not without causing more damage. You’re… tethered. Temporarily.”

Phainon pressed a hand to his chest, suddenly aware of that strange lightness again. Less weight. Less presence.

“That explains it,” he murmured.

Mydei’s jaw tightened. “Hyacine thought you were gone. She thought her own professor died and then the very person he was protecting also passed in the same breath.”

Phainon looked up sharply when Mydei met his gaze, “For a moment, she thought she’d lost both of you.”

He looked away, anger flickering hot and brief in his eyes. “Anaxagoras owes her answers. And apologies. A lot of them. You don’t tear yourself apart in front of someone who loves you and call it ‘necessary’ without consequences…” Mydei took another breath before continuing “Anaxa says you’re stable. Alive. Present. But altered.”

Phainon let out a shaky breath. “That’s… reassuring.”

“It’s not meant to be,” Mydei replied. “It’s meant to be a warning.”

He reached out again, fingers brushing Phainon’s wrist in a familiar, grounding gesture.

“So yes,” he said, voice firm. “You’re eating. Even if it burns. And then you’re resting. And then you’re staying.”

Phainon opened his eyes and nodded. “Okay.”

Mydei studied him for a long moment before turning back toward the hall. “Good. Because next time, I won't let anyone rip their soul apart for you.”

Phainon blinked. “Including you?”

Mydei didn’t answer.

He just started walking again, and Phainon followed.

Mydei’s touch burned in his hand. Not the sharp, painful kind. The unbearable kind that came with love, too bright to look at directly. Phainon found himself wondering, not for the first time, how many cycles he had loved him like this. Whether love itself carried over, even when memories didn’t. Whether it mattered if it did.

Did any of them remember the previous cycles?

He didn’t know. He knew very little, really. He’d been so wrapped up in surviving, in pulling himself back together piece by piece, that he hadn’t looked outward in a long time.

Instinctively, he reached inward.

He searched for that familiar pull. The quiet, steady presence that had always answered him. The thing that grounded him when everything else felt too loud or too sharp.

Nothing answered.

He tried again, focusing on the way Mydei guided him forward, on the familiar ache of longing that always came with his touch.

Nothing.

Phainon’s steps faltered.

His breath hitched, and then his hands started to shake. He didn’t know why at first. There was no pain. No warning. Just a sudden, awful emptiness where something vital had always been.

When Mydei glanced back and noticed the tremor in his grip, he stopped short. They were near a doorway now. Castorice’s, maybe. Phainon couldn’t tell. His back ached as if pulled too tight, his body drawn taut like a string about to snap.

“Khaslana,” he whispered inwardly.

Nothing answered.

“Khaslana?”

Still nothing.

Where are you?

Mydei turned fully then. His hand slid from Phainon’s shoulder to his neck, checking his pulse with quick, practiced precision, then up to his face, searching.

“Phainon?”

Phainon swallowed hard. His chest felt hollow, the air refusing to settle properly in his lungs.

“I… I don’t hear him,” he said, voice breaking despite his effort to keep it steady.

The words hung there, heavy and wrong, and for the first time since he woke, the fear truly set in.

Mydei tilted his head in that infuriatingly adoring way.

Phainon barely registered it.

Not when there was no fire in his core. Not when the familiar voice in his head was gone. Not when the barrier that had always held the weight of millions of cycles simply… wasn’t there anymore.

The cycles themselves blurred. Not slipping away. Not breaking. Just flattening into nothing, as if they had never existed at all.

He felt numb.

“Khaslana is gone,” Phainon whispered, panic clawing its way up his throat. “Where is he?”

His breath hitched as Mydei’s hands came up, warm and steady, cradling his face. Mydei’s expression twisted with confusion first, then worry, eyes searching him like something fragile had just cracked.

“Khaslana…?” Mydei repeated slowly. “Who is—”

He stopped, brows knitting together as if he were sorting through something just out of reach.

“Khaslana is…” He hesitated. “…you? Is he not?”

Phainon shook his head hard, the motion dizzying.

“No,” he gasped. “No—where is he? Where did he go?”

His legs tensed, instincts screaming at him to move, to run, to search. To find what had been taken. But there was nowhere to go. Nowhere to look.

There was only his own mind, and it was terrifyingly empty.

“I can’t feel him,” Phainon said, voice breaking completely now. “He was always there. Always.”

Mydei tightened his grip just enough to keep him grounded, thumbs brushing his cheekbones.

“Phainon,” he said carefully, urgently. “Stay with me. Look at me.”

Phainon tried.

But all he could feel was the absence.

His eyes burned.

He remembered the promise he had made to Khaslana. To himself. A vow carried across cycles and lives, whispered in moments when everything else was breaking. He had promised to save them. To save himself. Every version of him that had ever existed.

So why?

Where had he gone?

Mydei shifted closer and gently hooked an arm around him, steadying without trapping. “He’s still there,” he said quietly.

Phainon blinked up at him, disoriented. “But where…?”

Mydei exhaled, the sound heavy but measured. “If he is you,” he said slowly, “then as long as you’re here, he probably is too. Even if you can’t hear him right now.”

Phainon’s hands trembled again.

“So,” Mydei continued, voice firming just enough to anchor him, “you focus on taking care of yourself for a while. We’ll figure the rest out. Together. Like we always have.”

The words settled over him, not fixing the fear, but dulling its sharpest edge.

Phainon nodded and leaned into the touch, his forehead brushing Mydei’s shoulder. Mydei’s expression softened immediately, one hand coming up to cradle the back of his head.

It helped. More than Phainon wanted to admit.

He didn’t want to think about what his reaction might have been if Mydei hadn’t been there when he realized he couldn’t feel Khaslana. The thought alone made his chest tighten.

Phainon took a moment before they walked in.

Cipher looked up from where she was draped across Castorice’s furniture like she owned it. “Well, well,” she drawled. “The little prince and the little Deliverer boy finally grace us with their presence.”

She flashed a crooked smile, sharp as ever, though her eyes softened in a way that made Phainon’s chest ache. “Glad you decided to wake up.”

Castorice peeked out from the kitchen almost immediately, hands still damp as if she’d abandoned whatever she was doing the second she heard them. “Ah—Lord Phainon. Lord Mydei.” Relief washed over her features. “I’m glad you both made it. And that you’re back on your feet. Is your injury—”

Mydei lifted a hand, cutting her off. “It’s fine. I don’t go down easily.”

Phainon shot him a look that hovered somewhere between I forgot about that entirely and what do you mean injury.

Mydei very deliberately did not meet his eyes. “All healed up,” he added, glancing aside, “unlike a certain Deliverer.”

Cipher snorted. “You were stabbed, little prince.”

Phainon coughed “Mydeimos why are you even up–”

The words caught in Phainon’s throat before he could finish them.

His gaze had dropped, unthinking, and locked onto the chain around Mydei’s neck.

The ring.

Gorgo.

His breath stilled. His mother should still have been alive in Era Nova. She would have been. And yet the ring hanging there looked eerily familiar. Too familiar. It bore the same restored lines, the same subtle imperfections he remembered coaxing back into place with careful hands.

It could have been coincidence. Chartonus could simply have done excellent work.

But Phainon knew the difference between an original and a restoration. He always had.

His fingers curled faintly at his side.

So he kept it.

Mydei shifted, sensing the change even if he didn’t know why, but Phainon said nothing.

Castorice and Cipher shared a quick look.

“Ah—anyway,” Castorice said, clapping her hands once to redirect herself. “Lord Phainon, I know your taste buds are still… not ideal. But Hyacine said it’s important you eat properly to help with your physical recovery. Professor Anaxa plans to look over your internal recovery afterward, so for now you’re to follow Hyacine’s plan. Exactly.”

Phainon nodded without complaint. “Understood.”

He settled down beside Cipher and Mydei as Castorice moved about the room, happily setting plates out for everyone. When she handed him his, her fingers lingered for just a moment longer than necessary.

She could do that now.

The simple fact of it made something warm bloom in his chest, and he smiled without quite realizing it.

Cipher leaned over to inspect the food, humming thoughtfully. “Looks better than before, Princess Homebody. Your last attempt was—”

“Like death,” Castorice said promptly. “Yes. I know.”

Cipher grinned. “I was going to say bad, but if we’re being punny—”

“Please don’t,” Mydei muttered.

Phainon huffed a quiet laugh and lifted his utensils carefully. The food still radiated warmth, the kind he’d been dreading since Mydei mentioned eating. He braced himself anyway, shoulders tense, breath shallow.

The room felt full in a way it hadn’t in a long time. Voices overlapping softly. Familiar presences anchoring the space. Hands that reached out without fear, without hesitation.

He raised the food to his mouth and prepared for the bitterness.

Instead—

“…This tastes fine.”

The words slipped out before he could stop them.

He froze.

The flavor wasn’t sharp. It wasn’t burning. It wasn’t wrong. It was warm and solid and normal, settling on his tongue without protest.

By all rights, he should have been happy.

Relief should have followed. Gratitude. Some small, exhausted joy at another sign that he was healing.

Instead, dread curled tight in his chest.

Cold. Immediate. Absolute.

Khaslana.

The realization hit harder than any pain had. A part of him was missing. Not wounded. Not quiet. Gone. And the proof sat there on his tongue, undeniable.

The fire that should have reacted hadn’t stirred. No voice had risen in response. No presence had shifted to meet the sensation.

Phainon swallowed, hands trembling slightly as he lowered them back to the table.

The others were still talking. Still laughing. Still here.

And yet, all he could feel was the hollow terror of absence. The certainty that something essential had been taken from him and left no mark behind. No wound he could point to. No pain he could explain away.

Despite everything. Despite being alive. Despite being surrounded by people who cared.

Phainon could only feel dread.

I’m here. I’m alive. I can taste, he thought desperately. So why?

He set his utensils down with careful precision, as if any sudden movement might make the feeling worse. His stomach turned, not with hunger but with numbness, a sick, floating sensation that made his skin prickle. Phainon lifted a hand to his mouth, breathing shallowly. The nausea came in waves. It felt as though a portion of himself was missing, carved out cleanly and left behind. As if he had been spared too easily.

The thought made his chest tighten, and that awful sense of dread never lifted.

Khaslana was gone.

The truth settled into him like a weight he couldn’t shake, sinking deeper no matter how hard he tried to steady himself. No amount of warmth or safety could reach it. No familiar presence answered when he reached inward. No voice rose to meet his panic, no quiet reassurance to remind him he was still whole.

Phainon had failed.

He hadn’t woken up by accident. He hadn’t clawed his way back to consciousness out of instinct alone. He had woken because he willed himself to. Because he had made a choice.

He had wanted to save himself. He had wanted to save Khaslana. He had wanted to finally embrace the weight of millions of cycles instead of letting them blur and fracture.

He had wanted to live, not merely exist. To choose his own life. To give the life he wanted to others. To fulfill the promise he had carried across eras and endings.

That wish had been the anchor. The reason he’d endured the pain, the burning, the terror of unraveling. The reason he had reached forward instead of letting himself disappear.

And now—

Now the very thing he had woken up for was gone.

The failure curdled in his stomach, sharp and nauseating. It disgusted him in a way no physical pain ever could. If he couldn’t save himself, then what had any of it been for? If he couldn’t protect the part of him that mattered most, the part that had endured when everything else fell apart, then what right did he have to keep going?

The thought was quiet. Cold. Dangerous.

If I can’t save myself, he thought, trembling, why even live?

The question didn’t demand an answer.

It simply lingered, heavy and unresolved, as Phainon sat there surrounded by life and warmth, feeling more shattered apart than he ever had before.
